vignette:
He remembers the dust first. Not the sand of the desert, but the fine, pale grit that hung in the air after the mortar round hit the supply truck. He was twenty-two, a loader, barely a year in-country. The sound came a split second before the pressure wave-a crack that turned the world white and then silent, except for a high, thin ringing that stayed in his left ear for weeks. He remembers the smell of diesel fuel and burnt rubber, and the way the heat from the wreckage made his skin feel tight. He doesn't remember pulling the driver from the cab. He only knows his hands did it, because afterward they were red and raw from the metal. That afternoon is the one he keeps going back to, even now, almost forty years later.

On the warehouse floor, he moves between the racks of pallets with a practiced economy. His hands are always busy-stacking boxes, shrink-wrapping loads, checking inventory sheets. The forklift beeps in reverse, a high, repeated chirp that makes his shoulders climb toward his ears. He tells himself it's just a machine. But every time, his chest tightens, and he finds himself scanning the loading dock for cover that isn't there. The other workers have learned not to startle him. Once, a younger man clapped him on the back to ask a question, and he spun around with his fists up, heart hammering, ready to fight. He laughed it off afterward, said he was just jumpy. But he went home that evening and sat in the dark of his garage for an hour before going inside.

His partner, Rachel, knows the routine. She keeps the TV volume low. She doesn't walk up behind him. She learned not to touch his shoulder when he's asleep, because twice, he woke swinging, and once he gripped her wrist hard enough to leave bruises. He felt awful for weeks after that, and she didn't complain, which somehow made it worse. He tries to keep his nights quiet, but his brain won't cooperate. Around three in the morning, he jolts awake, gasping, convinced the ceiling is collapsing. The dream is always the same: he's back at the truck, and the driver is still inside, but he can't move his legs. He lies there in the dark, listening to his own breathing, until the streetlight through the blinds reassures him that he is in a bedroom, not a combat zone.

At work, he is reliable, never late, never sick. But he has a hard time with the loading dock supervisor, who barks orders over the intercom. The brusque tone-any tone that insists-floods him with an old anger. He has walked off the line twice, told to take a break, because he felt his jaw clench and his vision narrow. He doesn't understand why a raised voice still makes him want to hide or to strike. He just knows that his body remembers what his mind has tried to bury.

There are good days, too. Rachel makes a pot roast, and they watch old black-and-white movies. He laughs sometimes, genuinely. But even then, there is a vigilance he cannot drop. He sits with his back to the wall in restaurants. He checks the rearview mirror more than the road ahead. He keeps a tire iron under the passenger seat, though he can't say why. The world, he has learned, can turn violent in a second. The mortar round taught him that. What it didn't teach him was how to feel safe again.

He is sixty now. His back aches from the warehouse. His hands are calloused. And every single day, he carries that afternoon like a stone in his chest. He doesn't talk about it. He doesn't think about it on purpose. But the stone is there, heavy and familiar, and the dust never quite settles.
